(CNN) -- Jenny's phone number is for sale, but not for a song. "867-5309/Jenny" originally appeared on Tommy Tutone's "Tommy Tutone 2" album. Bids for a New Jersey version of the number, stuck in the minds of millions since Tommy Tutone's "867-5309/Jenny" hit the Top 10 in 1982, had reached $5,100 on eBay as of Monday morning. The song is about a guy who finds Jenny's name and number scribbled on a bathroom wall. "This is really, in my opinion, one of the last cultural remnants of the '80s pop culture era ... other than the mullet," said Spencer Potter, a 28-year-old DJ who is selling the number he got for free five years ago. While Potter is overlooking the fact that "867-5309" is an active phone number in dozens of other area codes, it does get called a lot by curious people. Potter said he has gotten about 40 calls a day since he got the area code 201 version for his Weehawken, New Jersey, DJ business. "The minute we plugged the phone jack into the wall, it began ringing," Potter said. Mostly, Potter said, the callers are "a lot of '80s fanatics" and he lets the calls ring through to his voice mail. When he did answer a call three years ago, Potter found his own Jenny on the line. "She had been using my number to give out to guys that she didn't like at bars," he said. "It was a bum phone number." The young lady from Hoboken, New Jersey, told Potter she was just curious about who might be getting the calls. Potter ended up asking her out. "I figured if she was having to give out a bum number that often then she was probably pretty cute," he said. "We ended up meeting for drinks. We dated for awhile and it was actually a great friendship." Potter recently moved from Weehawken and decided to try to make money off the infamous digits with an eBay auction. Potter's DJ business goes with the number, a necessary provision to get around phone company rules against selling telephone numbers, he said. Phone companies technically own the numbers, not the customers. Potter said Vonage, the company that assigned the number, gave him permission to transfer it as part of the sale of his business. EBay halted a 2004 auction by the purported holder of the 212 area code version of the number, The New York Times reported. A Philadelphia-area resident who holds the toll-free versions -- both 800 and 888 -- said he values his numbers in the millions. Jeffrey Steinberg said his best offer so far, rejected several years ago, was for $1 million from a national weight-loss company. He acquired the numbers in the early 1990s for a pizza delivery campaign and has licensed them for other advertisers in the years since. Potter said when his auction ends next Monday, February 9, he hopes to make at least $40,000. He said he would use the money to take a Caribbean vacation -- away from his ringing phone. . CNN's Laurie Segall and CNN Radio's April Williams contributed to this report.

(CNN) — Jenny’s phone number is being offered for purchase, though it is not going cheaply.

The number made famous by Tommy Tutone’s 1982 Top 10 hit “867-5309/Jenny,” first released on the band’s album *Tommy Tutone 2*, is up for auction in a New Jersey area code. By Monday morning, bidding on eBay had climbed to $5,100.

The song tells the story of a man who discovers Jenny’s name and phone number written on a bathroom wall. Decades later, the number remains lodged in popular memory.

“In my view, this is one of the last surviving pieces of ’80s pop culture — besides the mullet,” said Spencer Potter, a 28-year-old DJ who is selling the number he obtained at no cost five years earlier.

Potter is offering the 201-area-code version of the number, though “867-5309” is still assigned in many other area codes. Even so, his line receives plenty of calls from people curious about the famous digits.

Potter said that since acquiring the number for his DJ company in Weehawken, New Jersey, he has received about 40 calls a day.

“As soon as we plugged the phone line into the wall, it started ringing,” he said.

Most of the callers, Potter said, are “a lot of ’80s fanatics,” and he usually lets them go to voice mail. But when he answered one call three years ago, he encountered his own Jenny.

According to Potter, the woman had been handing out his number to men she met in bars but did not want to hear from again.

“She had been using my number to give out to guys that she didn’t like at bars,” he said. “It was a bum phone number.”

The woman, who was from Hoboken, New Jersey, told Potter she simply wanted to know who was receiving the calls. Potter then asked her out.

“I figured if she was having to give out a bum number that often then she was probably pretty cute,” he said.

The two met for drinks, dated for a time, and, Potter said, developed “a great friendship.”

After recently relocating from Weehawken, Potter decided to see whether he could profit from the well-known number by listing it on eBay. He said his DJ business is included with the number, a step he described as necessary to avoid phone company restrictions that prohibit the direct sale of telephone numbers.

Telephone numbers are technically owned by phone companies, not by customers. Potter said Vonage, which assigned him the number, allowed him to transfer it as part of the sale of his business.

The New York Times reported that in 2004, eBay stopped an auction by a person claiming to own the 212-area-code version of the number.

A man in the Philadelphia area who owns the toll-free versions — both 800 and 888 — said he believes his numbers are worth millions. Jeffrey Steinberg said the largest offer he has received was $1 million from a national weight-loss company, which he turned down several years ago.

Steinberg obtained the numbers in the early 1990s for a pizza delivery promotion and has since licensed them to other advertisers.

Potter said he hopes to earn at least $40,000 when his auction closes next Monday, February 9. He said he would spend the money on a Caribbean vacation — somewhere far from his constantly ringing phone.

CNN’s Laurie Segall and CNN Radio’s April Williams contributed to this report.

# 867-5309/Jenny: The Pop-Culture Phone Number That Became a Prank-Call Magnet and a Commercial Asset

Few phone numbers in American popular culture are as instantly recognizable as **867-5309**. Thanks to Tommy Tutone’s 1981 hit **“867-5309/Jenny,”** an ordinary seven-digit sequence became a national inside joke, a prank-call engine, and—under the right circumstances—a surprisingly valuable business asset.

The song’s hook is simple and unforgettable: a name, a number, and the implication that someone has scrawled both on a wall. More than four decades later, that number still carries cultural power. People remember it, sing it, dial it, and, in some cases, try to profit from it.

## A Number Turned Into a Cultural Artifact

“867-5309/Jenny” became famous because it fused two things people remember easily: a catchy chorus and a realistic phone number. Unlike fictional numbers using the traditional **“555”** exchange, 867-5309 looked and sounded real. That realism was part of the appeal—and part of the problem.

After the song became a hit, people across the United States began dialing **867-5309** in their own area codes, hoping to reach “Jenny.” Many reached ordinary households and businesses instead. Some recipients reported waves of prank calls, hang-ups, late-night singing, and requests to “speak to Jenny.”

The number became a kind of shared pop-culture dare: if you knew the song, you knew the number; if you had a phone, you could test whether Jenny existed.

## The Prank-Call Problem

For people who happened to have 867-5309 as their phone number, the joke often became exhausting. In virtually every area code where the number was active, it had the potential to attract callers. Some people changed their numbers to escape the nuisance. Others leaned into it, using voicemail greetings that referenced the song or turning the notoriety into free publicity.

The prank-call phenomenon also revealed something important about pre-smartphone culture: phone numbers were once more public, more personal, and more permanent. A memorable number could become part of someone’s identity—or an unwanted burden. With “867-5309,” the boundary between entertainment and harassment was often thin.

For businesses, however, the same quality that annoyed private individuals could be valuable. A number that customers already remembered had built-in advertising power.

## Commercial Value: Why 867-5309 Is Worth Money

A phone number can be commercially valuable if it is:

- easy to remember,
- connected to a familiar phrase or song,
- useful for advertising,
- rare within a desirable area code, and
- capable of generating attention on its own.

By those standards, **867-5309** is one of the strongest vanity-style numbers in North America. It is not a traditional vanity number like 1-800-FLOWERS, but it functions similarly because the public already knows it.

Businesses have used versions of 867-5309 for marketing, especially in industries where memorability matters: plumbing, towing, radio, entertainment, restaurants, and local services. A company with that number can put it on a sign or commercial and trust that many people will recognize it immediately.

The number also benefits from nostalgia. For customers who grew up with the song, seeing 867-5309 can create a quick emotional connection. It signals humor, familiarity, and cultural awareness.

## The eBay Auction and the Question of “Owning” a Number

The commercial value of 867-5309 became especially clear when versions of the number appeared in online auctions, including on **eBay**. One widely discussed auction involved a person or business offering a phone number ending in 867-5309, often bundled with a business or service arrangement rather than sold as a standalone object.

That distinction matters. In the United States and Canada, phone numbers are generally **not private property** in the way a car, domain name, or collectible is. Subscribers typically do not “own” their phone numbers. Instead, numbers are assigned by phone companies under regulatory rules, and customers have the right to use them as long as service remains active and rules are followed.

Because of that, phone companies usually prohibit the direct sale of a phone number by itself. A customer cannot simply say, “I own 867-5309 and I’m selling it to the highest bidder.” The carrier controls assignment and transfer procedures.

This is why auctions involving famous phone numbers often become legally and logistically complicated. Sellers may try to structure the deal as the sale of a business, a customer list, a service contract, or some other asset that includes the phone number as part of the transfer. Even then, the transfer generally depends on carrier approval.

In other words, the market may believe the number has value, but the phone company’s rules determine whether that value can actually be realized.

## Phone Company Rules: Why Famous Numbers Are Hard to Sell

Phone numbers are part of the North American Numbering Plan, a shared system managed through carriers and regulators. The purpose of the system is to ensure that numbers are assigned fairly, efficiently, and reliably.

Common carrier rules and policies often include:

- customers do not own numbers outright;
- numbers cannot usually be sold independently;
- transfers must follow carrier procedures;
- a number may be reassigned if service is disconnected;
- portability rules allow customers to move numbers between carriers, but not to treat them as unrestricted property;
- businesses may transfer numbers during mergers, acquisitions, or account changes, subject to approval.

These rules are designed to prevent speculation, hoarding, fraud, and confusion. If popular numbers could be freely bought and sold, memorable combinations could become commodities, creating a secondary market that regulators and carriers have historically been reluctant to encourage.

That said, businesses routinely benefit from memorable numbers. The line between “using” a valuable number and “selling” a valuable number is where disputes often arise.

## From Annoyance to Asset

The story of 867-5309 is unusual because the same feature created both nuisance and value. For a private person, the number could mean endless prank calls. For a business, it could mean instant recognition.

A homeowner might hear, “Is Jenny there?” fifty times and call the phone company to change the number. A business owner might hear the same thing and realize they have a marketing tool. The number’s value depends almost entirely on context.

That dual identity explains why 867-5309 has remained fascinating. It is not just a lyric. It is a case study in how popular culture can attach meaning to ordinary infrastructure. A random phone number became a joke, a burden, an advertising device, and an auction item.

## Why 867-5309 Still Matters

Today, many people communicate through texts, apps, and social media rather than dialing landlines. Yet 867-5309 still survives as a cultural reference. It appears in advertisements, jokes, business names, trivia nights, and nostalgic radio segments.

Its staying power comes from the fact that it belongs to a rare category: a fictional-seeming number that became real in thousands of places. Every area code offered the possibility that Jenny might answer.

The eBay auctions and carrier disputes only added to the legend. They showed that a phone number could have celebrity status—and even market value—without being ownable in the traditional sense.

## Conclusion

**867-5309/Jenny** is more than a catchy chorus. It is one of the best examples of a pop song escaping into everyday life. It transformed a simple phone number into a national prank, a source of frustration for unsuspecting subscribers, and a potentially valuable commercial asset.

The number’s history also highlights an important legal and practical reality: phone numbers can be culturally priceless and commercially useful, but they are still governed by phone company rules. You may be able to use a famous number, advertise with it, or transfer it as part of a business arrangement—but you usually cannot simply own and sell it like a piece of property.

That tension is exactly what makes 867-5309 so enduring. It belongs to everyone who remembers the song, to no one completely, and to “Jenny” most of all.

*CNN-style news piece — 2009*

**By CNN Staff**  
**March 2009**

For anyone who grew up with the 1980s hit “867-5309/Jenny” stuck in their head, one phone number has always stood out from the rest.

Now, decades after Tommy Tutone’s pop-rock anthem turned seven digits into a national punchline, one owner of the famous number is trying to cash in.

An online auction for a phone number ending in **867-5309** has drawn bids as high as **$5,100**, according to the seller, who says he never expected a familiar lyric to turn into a potential payday.

“I knew people recognized it right away,” the seller told CNN. “Every time I gave out the number, somebody would sing it back to me. But I didn’t think it would become something people would actually bid thousands of dollars for.”

The number, attached to a local phone exchange, has been listed as a novelty item for businesses, collectors or die-hard fans of the 1982 song, which famously repeats the line: “Jenny, I got your number.”

But owning the number can be more complicated than simply enjoying a pop culture relic.

Several people across the United States who have had some version of **867-5309** say the number brings a steady stream of prank calls, late-night singalongs and curious strangers asking for Jenny.

“It’s funny the first couple of times,” said one longtime owner of a similar number in the Midwest. “Then it’s 2 a.m. and someone’s yelling the chorus into your voicemail. After that, it gets old pretty quickly.”

Another owner, who uses the number for a small business, said the notoriety can actually help.

“People don’t forget it,” he said. “That’s the whole point. If you’re trying to advertise, it’s probably one of the easiest numbers in America to remember.”

The song’s enduring fame has made the number one of the most recognizable in pop music history. Since its release, people assigned 867-5309 in various area codes have reported everything from harmless jokes to constant harassment. In some places, phone companies reportedly avoided issuing the number altogether because of the volume of unwanted calls.

The current seller says he sees the auction as a chance to put the number in the hands of someone who wants it — and understands what comes with it.

“I’m not selling a regular phone number,” he said. “I’m selling a piece of the ’80s.”

Whether the winning bidder plans to use it for a business, a collection or simply bragging rights remains unclear. But with bids already topping $5,000, one thing is certain: Jenny’s number still gets plenty of attention.
